title: Indian Students Face New Form Requirements for US Visa Extensions From September
excerpt: Starting September 15, F-1 students must file Form I-539 with USCIS and provide biometrics to extend their stay, replacing the previous school-managed process.
body:
• F-1 students must file Form I-539 directly with USCIS to extend their stay, instead of relying on school officials to update SEVIS records.
  • The Form I-94 "admit until" date becomes the controlling document for lawful stay, replacing the open-ended Duration of Status framework.
  • Students applying for OPT or STEM OPT after March 18, 2027 will need to file both Form I-765 and Form I-539 simultaneously.
  • International travel while an extension application is pending may trigger case abandonment.

What Is Changing

Starting September 15, Indian students on F-1 visas in the United States will face a new set of form-filing requirements to extend their stay. The Department of Homeland Security's final rule, published in the Federal Register on July 17, replaces the longstanding Duration of Status framework with fixed admission periods and mandatory extension procedures.

The most immediate change: extending a stay beyond the admit-until date on Form I-94 will now require filing Form I-539, Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status, directly with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Previously, a school's designated school official could simply extend a student's program end date in the federal SEVIS database, and that was legally sufficient to maintain lawful status, according to Nolo.

Form I-94 Becomes the Controlling Document

Under the new framework, the Form I-94 "admit-until" date — not the Form I-20 program end date — becomes the document that legally controls a student's authorized stay. F-1 students will be admitted for the length of their program, capped at four years, with a 30-day pre-arrival period and a 30-day post-completion period, according to the DHS final rule.

The post-completion grace period has been cut from 60 days to 30 days, giving students less time to arrange departure, transfer to a higher degree program, or apply for a change of status after completing their studies.

New Extension Filing Process

Students who need additional time to complete their degree, begin a new program, or pursue Optional Practical Training must file Form I-539 with USCIS, pay the filing fee, and provide biometrics. Applications may also require proof of sufficient financial resources and, in some cases, a field office interview, according to Capitol Immigration Law Group.

"Program extensions issued by a Designated School Official will no longer extend your legal immigration status."

— Capitol Immigration Law Group

Students with timely filed, pending extension applications may continue studying while USCIS reviews the request. On-campus work authorization and off-campus employment based on severe economic hardship may be auto-extended for up to 240 days while an extension is pending.

OPT and STEM OPT: Dual Filing Ahead

A temporary reprieve allows F-1 students already in Duration of Status who file Form I-765 for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT on or before March 18, 2027, to avoid a separate extension application. After that deadline, students will need to file both Form I-765 for employment authorization and Form I-539 for an extension of stay if the practical training period extends beyond their fixed I-94 date.

The standard 180-day automatic work authorization extension for timely filed STEM OPT requests remains unchanged.

Travel Risks and Transition Rules

International travel becomes significantly more complex. Departing the United States while an extension or change-of-status application is pending will generally result in the application being deemed abandoned by USCIS. Any international travel on or after September 15 will terminate existing Duration of Status, and the student will receive a fixed-date I-94 upon re-entry.

Students currently in the US under Duration of Status may remain until their I-20 program end date or November 14, 2030, whichever comes first.

Impact on Indian Students

India is one of the largest sources of F-1 students in the United States. The new requirements add both costs and administrative complexity, particularly for students in programs that commonly extend beyond four years, such as doctoral research and medical training.

The Association of American Medical Colleges has warned that the new hurdles could make it harder for international students to complete medical degrees and biomedical research programs, according to the American Institute of Physics. Research universities have raised concerns that the rule may not reflect the realities of advanced training, where laboratory work, clinical requirements, and other academic changes often push programs past the four-year cap.

The rule also prohibits students who complete a degree at one level from enrolling in a program at the same or lower level — ending the common strategy of enrolling in a second master's program to access Curricular Practical Training after an unsuccessful H-1B lottery.

What Students Should Do Now

Immigration attorneys recommend reviewing Form I-94 expiration dates carefully, coordinating with school officials well before the September 15 effective date, and avoiding international travel while any extension application is pending. Students nearing the end of a program should file for extensions or OPT early to build in processing time.
nri_angle: Indian F-1 students — one of the largest international student populations in the US — face new paperwork, biometrics, and filing fees to extend their stays, with particular impact on PhD and medical students in programs exceeding four years.
